paragraphs: Priam ransoms the body of Hector—Hector’s funeral.

The assembly broke up, and the people scattered, each man to his own ship. There they prepared their supper and turned their thoughts to the welcome gift of sleep. But Achilles kept weeping for his dear comrade, and sleep, to whom all things submit, would not take hold of him. He tossed from one side to the other, longing for the strength and manliness of Patroclus. He remembered everything they had done together and everything they had endured, in battle and on the waves of the wearying sea. As he dwelt on these memories he wept bitterly. He lay first on his side, then on his back, then face down, until at last he got up and went out like a man out of his mind to wander along the shore. When he saw dawn breaking over the beach and the sea, he harnessed his horses to his chariot and tied the body of Hector behind it to drag it along. Three times he dragged it around the tomb of the son of Menoetius. Then he went back into his tent and left the body lying on the ground, stretched out full length and face down. But Apollo would not allow it to be disfigured. He pitied the man, dead though he was, and so he kept covering him with his golden aegis, so that Hector would come to no harm while Achilles dragged him.

In this way Achilles, in his fury, shamefully dishonored Hector. The blessed gods looked down from heaven in pity, and they urged Hermes, slayer of Argus, to steal the body. All of them agreed except Hera, Poseidon, and Zeus’s gray-eyed daughter. They held on to the hatred they had always felt for Ilium, for Priam and his people. They had never forgiven the wrong Paris did them, when the goddesses came to him in his sheepyards and he scorned them, favoring instead the one who offered him a wanton woman, to his ruin.

When the morning of the twelfth day came, Phoebus Apollo spoke among the immortals. “You gods should be ashamed of yourselves. You are cruel and hard-hearted. Did Hector not burn thigh-bones of heifers and unblemished goats for you? Yet now you do not dare to rescue even his dead body, so that his wife could look on it, with his mother and his child, his father Priam, and his people, who would burn him at once and give him his proper funeral rites. So all of you would rather take the side of raging Achilles, who knows neither right nor pity? He is like a savage lion that, proud of its great strength and daring, springs on men’s flocks and gorges itself on them. In the same way Achilles has thrown away all pity, and all that conscience which does a man great harm and great good if he heeds it. A man may lose someone far dearer than Achilles has lost—a son, perhaps, or a brother born from his own mother’s womb. Yet when he has mourned and wept for him, he lets him rest, for it takes a great deal of sorrow to kill a man. But Achilles, now that he has killed noble Hector, drags him behind his chariot around the tomb of his comrade. It would be more honorable of him, and better for him, not to do this. Brave though he is, we gods may take offense when he vents his fury on dead clay.”

Hera answered angrily. “That would be fine, lord of the silver bow,” she cried, “if you would give Hector and Achilles equal honor. But Hector was mortal and nursed at a woman’s breast, while Achilles is the child of a goddess, one I raised and brought up myself. I gave her in marriage to Peleus, who is exceedingly dear to the immortals. All of you gods came to her wedding. You feasted there with them yourself, and you brought your lyre—you who have always been false, and fond of bad company.”

Then Zeus said, “Hera, do not be so bitter. Their honor will not be equal. But of all who live in Ilium, Hector was the dearest to the gods, and to me as well, because his offerings never failed me. My altar was never short of its dues, or of the drink-offerings and the savor of sacrifice, which we claim as our right. So I will allow mighty Hector’s body to be stolen. But this can hardly be done without Achilles finding out, for his mother stays beside him night and day. Let one of you send Thetis to me, and I will give her my counsel: Achilles is to accept a ransom from Priam and give up the body.”

At this Iris, swift as the wind, went off to deliver Zeus’s message. She plunged down into the dark sea midway between Samos and rocky Imbrus. The water hissed as it closed over her, and she sank to the bottom like the lead on an ox-horn line, which speeds down to bring death to fishes. She found Thetis sitting in a great cave, with the other sea-goddesses gathered around her. In the midst of them she sat weeping for her noble son, who was to fall far from his own land, on the rich plains of Troy. Iris went up to her and said, “Rise, Thetis. Zeus, whose counsels never fail, calls you to him.” Thetis answered, “Why does the mighty god call me? I am in great grief, and I shrink from moving among the immortals. Still, I will go, and whatever word he speaks will not be spoken in vain.”

The goddess took her dark veil, the most somber robe there is, and set out, with swift Iris leading the way. The waves of the sea parted to make a path for them. When they reached the shore they flew up into the heavens, where they found the all-seeing son of Cronus with the blessed gods who live forever gathered around him. Athena gave up her seat to Thetis, and she sat down beside father Zeus. Hera then put a fair golden cup in her hand and spoke words of comfort to her. Thetis drank and handed the cup back, and the father of gods and men was the first to speak.

“So, goddess,” he said, “despite all your sorrow, and the grief that I know well fills your heart always, you have come here to Olympus. I will tell you why I sent for you. For nine days now the immortals have been quarreling over Achilles, the waster of cities, and the body of Hector. The gods wanted Hermes, slayer of Argus, to steal the body. But to further our peace and friendship from now on, I will grant your son an honor, which I will now tell you. Go to the army and lay these commands on him. Tell him that the gods are angry with him, and that I am angrier than all of them, because he keeps Hector at the ships and will not give him up. Perhaps he will fear me and let the body go. At the same time I will send Iris to great Priam, to tell him to go to the ships of the Achaeans and ransom his son, bringing gifts for Achilles that will satisfy him.”

Silver-footed Thetis did as the god had told her. At once she darted down from the topmost summits of Olympus. She went to her son’s tents and found him grieving bitterly, while his faithful comrades around him were busy preparing their morning meal, for which they had killed a great woolly sheep. His mother sat down beside him and stroked him with her hand. “My son,” she said, “how long will you go on grieving and moaning like this? You are gnawing at your own heart, and you think neither of food nor of a woman’s embrace. Yet these things too are good, for you have not long to live, and death and strong-handed fate are already close beside you. Now listen to what I say, for I come as a messenger from Zeus. He says that the gods are angry with you, and that he is angrier than all of them, because you keep Hector at the ships and will not give him up. So let him go, and accept a ransom for his body.”
Achilles answered, “So be it. If Olympian Zeus of his own will commands this, then let the man who brings the ransom carry the body away.”

So mother and son spoke together at the ships, at long length. Meanwhile the son of Cronus sent Iris to the strong city of Ilium. “Go, swift Iris,” he said, “from the mansions of Olympus, and tell King Priam in Ilium to go to the ships of the Achaeans and free the body of his dear son. He is to take gifts with him that will satisfy Achilles. He is to go alone, with no other Trojan, except some honored servant who can drive his mules and wagon and bring back the body of the man whom noble Achilles has killed. Let him have no thought or fear of death in his heart, for we will send the slayer of Argus to escort him and bring him into Achilles’s tent. Achilles will not kill him or let anyone else do it. He will be careful in his conduct and do no wrong, and he will treat a suppliant with all honorable courtesy.”

At this Iris, swift as the wind, sped off to deliver her message. She came to Priam’s house and found weeping and lamentation inside. His sons sat around their father in the outer courtyard, their clothes wet with tears. The old man sat among them wrapped tightly in his mantle, his head and neck covered with the filth he had clutched up as he lay groveling in the mire. His daughters and his sons’ wives went wailing through the house, thinking of the many brave men who lay dead, killed by the Argives. The messenger of Zeus stood beside Priam and spoke gently to him, but fear came over him as she did. “Take heart, Priam, offspring of Dardanus,” she said. “Take heart and do not be afraid. I bring no evil news; I mean well toward you. I come as a messenger from Zeus, who is far away but cares for you and pities you. The lord of Olympus tells you to go and ransom noble Hector, taking gifts that will satisfy Achilles. You are to go alone, with no Trojan, except some honored servant who can drive your mules and wagon and bring back to the city the body of the man whom noble Achilles has killed. You are to have no thought or fear of death, for Zeus will send the slayer of Argus to escort you. When he has brought you into Achilles’s tent, Achilles will not kill you or let anyone else do it. He will be careful in his conduct and do no wrong, and he will treat a suppliant with all honorable courtesy.”

When she had spoken, Iris went on her way. Priam told his sons to get a mule-wagon ready and to fasten the wagon body firmly on top of its frame. Then he went down into his fragrant storeroom, high-vaulted and made of cedar, where his many treasures were kept, and called his wife Hecuba. “Wife,” he said, “a messenger has come to me from Olympus and has told me to go to the ships of the Achaeans and ransom my dear son, taking gifts that will satisfy Achilles. What do you think of this? For my own part, I am strongly drawn to go through the camps of the Achaeans and to their ships.”

His wife cried out when she heard him. “Alas,” she said, “what has become of the good judgment for which you have always been famous, among strangers and your own people? How can you dare to go alone to the ships of the Achaeans and look in the face of the man who has killed so many of your brave sons? You must have a heart of iron. If that cruel savage sees you and lays hands on you, he will show neither respect nor pity. Let us weep for Hector from afar, here in our own house. When I gave birth to him, the threads of overruling fate were spun for him so that dogs would eat his flesh far from his parents, in the house of that terrible man. I would gladly fasten on his liver and devour it. That is how I would avenge my son, who showed no cowardice when Achilles killed him, and thought neither of flight nor of avoiding battle as he stood defending the Trojan men and Trojan women.”

Then Priam said, “I will go. Do not try to stop me, and do not be a bird of ill omen in my house, for you will not move me. If some mortal man had sent me—a prophet or a priest who reads the future from sacrifice—I would have thought him false and paid him no heed. But now I have heard the goddess and seen her face to face. So I will go, and her word will not be spoken in vain. If it is my fate to die at the ships of the Achaeans, so I would have it. Let Achilles kill me, if only I can first take my son in my arms and mourn him until my heart is comforted.”

With these words he lifted the lids of his chests and took out twelve fine robes. He also took twelve single-fold cloaks, twelve rugs, twelve fair mantles, and the same number of shirts. He weighed out ten talents of gold, and brought two burnished tripods, four cauldrons, and a very beautiful cup that the Thracians had given him when he went to them on an embassy. It was very precious, but he did not begrudge even this, so eager was he to ransom his son’s body. Then he drove all the Trojans out of the courtyard, scolding them angrily. “Get out,” he cried, “you shame and disgrace to me. Have you no grief in your own homes, that you come to pester me here? Do you think it a small thing that the son of Cronus has sent this sorrow on me, the loss of the bravest of my sons? No, you will find it out yourselves, for now that he is gone the Achaeans will have an easier time killing you. As for me, let me go down into the house of Hades before my eyes see the sacking and wasting of the city.”

He drove the men away with his staff, and they left as the old man hurried them. Then he called to his sons, scolding Helenus, Paris, noble Agathon, Pammon, Antiphonus, Polites of the loud battle cry, Deiphobus, Hippothous, and Dius. These nine the old man called to him. “Come to me at once,” he cried, “you worthless sons who shame me. I wish you had all been killed at the ships instead of Hector. Miserable man that I am, I had the bravest sons in all Troy—noble Nestor, Troilus the dauntless charioteer, and Hector, who was a god among men, so that one would have thought him the son of an immortal. Yet not one of them is left. Ares has killed them, and the ones I am ashamed of are all that remain to me. Liars, and light on your feet, heroes of the dance, robbers of lambs and kids from your own people, why do you not get a wagon ready for me at once and load all these things on it, so that I can set out on my way?”

So he spoke, and they feared their father’s rebuke. They brought out a strong mule-wagon, newly made, and fastened the wagon body on its frame. They took the mule-yoke down from its peg, a boxwood yoke with a knob on top and rings for the reins to pass through. Then they brought out a yoke-band eleven cubits long to bind the yoke to the pole. They tied it on at the far end of the pole and put the ring over the upright pin, fastening it with three turns of the band on each side of the knob and bending the thong of the yoke beneath it. When this was done, they brought the rich ransom for Hector’s body out of the storeroom and set it all in order on the wagon. Then they yoked the strong harness-mules that the Mysians had once given Priam as a fine present. For Priam himself they yoked horses that the old king had bred and kept for his own use.

Priam and his servant carefully finished yoking their carriages at the palace. Then Hecuba came up to them, heavy with sorrow, carrying a golden goblet of wine in her right hand so that they could pour a drink-offering before leaving. She stopped in front of the horses and said, “Take this and pour a drink-offering to father Zeus. You are determined to go to the ships against my wishes, so pray that you return safely from the hands of your enemies. Pray to the son of Cronus, lord of the whirlwind, who sits on Ida and looks down over all Troy. Ask him to send his swift messenger to your right, the bird of omen that is strongest and dearest to him of all birds, so that you see it with your own eyes and can trust it as you set out for the ships of the Danaans. If all-seeing Zeus will not send you this messenger, then however set on going you may be, I would not have you approach the ships of the Argives.”
Priam answered, “Wife, I will do as you ask. It is good to lift hands in prayer to Zeus, in case he may have mercy on me.”

With this the old man told the serving-woman to pour pure water over his hands. She came with the water in a bowl, and he washed his hands and took the cup from his wife. Standing in the middle of the courtyard with his eyes turned to heaven, he poured the drink-offering and prayed. “Father Zeus,” he said, “you who rule from Ida, most glorious and most great, let me find a kind and compassionate welcome in the tents of Achilles. Send your swift messenger to my right, the bird of omen that is strongest and dearest to you of all birds, so that I see it with my own eyes and can trust it as I set out for the ships of the Danaans.”

So he prayed, and Zeus, lord of counsel, heard his prayer. At once he sent an eagle, the most unerring portent of all flying birds, the dusky hunter that men also call the Black Eagle. Its wings spread out on either side as wide as the well-made, well-bolted door of a rich man’s chamber. It came flying over the city on their right, and when they saw it they were glad, and their hearts took comfort. The old man hurried to mount his chariot and drove out through the inner gateway and under the echoing gatehouse of the outer court. In front went the mules pulling the four-wheeled wagon, driven by wise Idaeus. Behind them came the horses, which the old man lashed with his whip and drove quickly through the city, while his friends followed, wailing and lamenting for him as though he were on his way to death. As soon as they had come down from the city and reached the plain, his sons and sons-in-law, who had followed him, turned back to Ilium.

But Priam and Idaeus, as they came into view on the plain, did not escape the notice of all-seeing Zeus, who looked down at the old man and pitied him. He spoke to his son Hermes. “Hermes,” he said, “you are the one who most likes to escort men on their way, and you listen to whomever you choose. Go, and guide Priam to the ships of the Achaeans in such a way that none of the other Danaans will see him or notice him until he reaches the son of Peleus.”

So he spoke, and Hermes, guide and guardian, slayer of Argus, did as he was told. At once he tied on his glittering golden sandals, with which he could fly like the wind over land and sea. He took the wand with which he closes men’s eyes in sleep or wakes them whenever he pleases, and flew with it in his hand until he came to Troy and the Hellespont. To look at, he was like a young man of noble birth in the prime of his youth and beauty, with the first down just coming on his face.

Now when Priam and Idaeus had driven past the great tomb of Ilus, they halted their mules and horses to let them drink in the river, for the shades of night were falling. Then Idaeus saw Hermes standing near them and said to Priam, “Take care, descendant of Dardanus. This is a matter that needs thought. I see a man who I think will attack us at any moment. Let us flee with our horses, or at least embrace his knees and beg him to have compassion on us.”

When the old man heard this, his heart failed him and he was in great fear. He stayed where he was as if dazed, and the hair stood on end all over his body. But the bringer of good luck came up, took him by the hand, and said, “Where, father, are you driving your mules and horses like this, in the dead of night, when other men are asleep? Are you not afraid of the fierce Achaeans, so cruel and relentless, who are close by? If one of them saw you carrying so much treasure through the darkness of the rushing night, what would become of you? You are no longer young, and the man with you is too old to protect you from those who would attack you. As for me, I will do you no harm, and I will defend you against anyone else, for you remind me of my own father.”

Priam answered, “It is just as you say, my dear son. Still, some god has held his hand over me, since he has sent such a traveler as you to meet me at such a good moment. You are so handsome in looks and figure, and your judgment is so sound, that you must come from blessed parents.”

Then the slayer of Argus, guide and guardian, said, “Sir, everything you have said is right. But tell me, and tell me truly: are you sending this rich treasure to a foreign people, where it may be safe? Or are you all abandoning strong Ilium in dismay now that your son has fallen, who was the bravest man among you and never lacked courage in battle with the Achaeans?”
Priam asked, “Who are you, my friend, and who are your parents? How is it that you speak so truly of the fate of my unhappy son?”

The slayer of Argus, guide and guardian, answered him. “Sir, you are testing me when you question me about noble Hector. Many a time I have seen him in battle, driving the Argives to their ships and putting them to the sword. We stood still and marveled, because Achilles, in his anger with the son of Atreus, did not let us fight. I am his squire, and I came with him in the same ship. I am a Myrmidon, and my father’s name is Polyctor. He is a rich man and about as old as you are. He has six sons besides me, and I am the seventh. We cast lots, and it fell to me to sail here with Achilles. I have now come from the ships onto the plain, because at daybreak the Achaeans will set up their battle lines around the city. They are restless from doing nothing and so eager that their princes cannot hold them back.”
